708.title: Job loses everything
708.hook: a good man loses his children, wealth and health (Job 1–2)
708.howItsDone: Jews and Christians read the book of Job as scripture, and it is often read or studied in times of grief and loss; readers in both traditions interpret its opening in different ways.

segments.voice: Yesterday: eight parts of a path, the Buddha's fourth truth. Your line was one step of eight. Which step did the day hand you? Today the question of suffering moves to another house: the book of Job. Day seven hundred eight.

"There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job." The book opens like a folk tale, plain and quick. And before anything happens to him, it tells us what kind of man he is: "perfect and upright, and one that feared God, and eschewed evil." Hold on to that line. The whole book leans on it. The story is about to take everything this man has, and it wants the reader to know, before a single loss, that he did nothing to earn it.
screen: `A MAN IN THE LAND OF UZ.` → `PERFECT AND UPRIGHT.` → `BEFORE A SINGLE LOSS.`

segments.voice: First, a full house. Job has sons and daughters, flocks and herds, and a large household. His children hold feasts in each other's homes, and afterward Job rises early to make offerings for them, in case one of them sinned in their heart. A careful father, worried for his kids. Second, a scene Job never sees. The story moves to heaven, and a figure the King James calls Satan puts a question to God: "Doth Job fear God for nought?" Take away what he has, the figure says, and see what he does. God allows it. Nowhere in the book is Job told about this conversation. Not in chapter one, and not at the end. Third, the messengers. On one day, messengers come running, and each is still speaking when the next arrives. Raiders took the oxen and the donkeys. Fire fell and burned the sheep. Raiders took the camels. And a great wind struck the house where his sons and daughters were eating, and they died. Job tears his robe, shaves his head, falls to the ground, and says: "the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD." Then chapter two takes his body too: sores from the soles of his feet to the top of his head. He sits down among the ashes and scrapes himself with a piece of broken pottery. Fourth, it wasn't deserved. The book tells the reader, and not Job, that none of this is punishment. God himself calls Job his servant, a perfect and an upright man. So whatever explanations arrive in the chapters ahead, the reader has already been told this much. Jews and Christians both read Job as scripture, and they read it in many ways. But the book itself starts here: a good man, and losses he did not earn.
screen: `A FULL HOUSE, A CAREFUL FATHER.` · `A SCENE JOB NEVER SEES.` · `THE MESSENGERS, ONE AFTER ANOTHER.` · `THE READER KNOWS: NOT PUNISHMENT.` · then, large: `IT WASN'T DESERVED.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the body be heavy for a moment. Bring to mind someone carrying a pain they didn't earn. An illness, an accident, a loss that came out of nowhere. It might be you. Picture them as the book pictures Job at the end of chapter two: sitting down, in the ashes, with what's left. The reader of Job is told one thing that Job is not. So be that reader for a moment. Over the person you're picturing, say the line inwardly, once, slowly: it wasn't deserved. Then just stay beside them, the way you'd stay beside someone sitting on the ground. The bell holds the time.
Job loses everything: in the opening chapters of Job, a blameless man loses his children, his wealth and his health, and the reader is told it isn't punishment. Today's word.

Your line: it wasn't deserved. Today, if you hear someone blaming themselves for a trouble they didn't cause, or catch yourself doing it, say the line once, aloud or inside: it wasn't deserved. Day seven hundred eight.

what a scholar hears: the book's frame: the reader overhears the heavenly scenes (Job 1:6–12; 2:1–6), and Job never does, so his whole argument happens without them.

709.title: Seven days of silence
709.hook: his friends sit silent with him seven days, their finest hour (Job 2:13)
709.howItsDone: Some Jewish and Christian readers take Job 2:11–13 as a picture of comforting mourners; in Jewish mourning custom, visitors come to sit with the bereaved, and tradition has visitors wait for the mourner to speak first.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Job loses everything, and the reader is told first that it wasn't punishment. Your line was it wasn't deserved. Did you catch your mind hunting for someone's fault, and let it go? Today, his friends arrive. Day seven hundred nine.

At a wake, a slow line of people moves past the family. Each one leans in and says something. I'm so sorry. She was a lovely woman. Call me if you need anything. Then somebody reaches the front, takes a hand in both of theirs, and says nothing at all. Just holds on, and stays a moment, and moves along. Saying nothing can be the hardest thing in that line to do. In the book of Job, three friends do exactly that, and for a long time.
screen: `A SLOW LINE AT A WAKE.` → `SOMEONE SAYS NOTHING AT ALL.` → `THREE FRIENDS DO EXACTLY THAT.`

segments.voice: First, they come. Three of Job's friends, Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar, hear about everything that has fallen on him. Each sets out from his own place, and the text says they had made an appointment together "to come to mourn with him and to comfort him." Before a word is said, there's this: they make a plan, and they travel. Second, they don't know him. From far off they look up and can't recognize their friend. The man on the ash heap doesn't look like Job anymore. So they raise their voices and weep. Each tears his robe. They throw dust into the air, over their heads, toward heaven. Their mourning is loud and physical, before it's anything else. Third, they sit down. Here's the verse: "So they sat down with him upon the ground seven days and seven nights, and none spake a word unto him: for they saw that his grief was very great." Notice where they sit: upon the ground, with him, at his level, not standing over him. And notice how long. Day and night, and nobody fills the air. Fourth, silence that comes from seeing. The verse gives one reason for the quiet: they saw. They looked at their friend and saw how great the grief was. Some readers take it that words would have been too small for it. Some call this the friends' finest hour, partly because of what happens when they finally open their mouths. But that's tomorrow. For now, the text gives them only this: they came, they wept, they sat on the ground where he was, and they kept their mouths shut because they could see.
screen: `THEY COME, BY APPOINTMENT.` · `THEY CAN'T RECOGNIZE HIM.` · `THEY SIT ON THE GROUND WITH HIM.` · `SILENCE THAT COMES FROM SEEING.` · then, large: `SIT WITH THEM.`

segments.voice: Settle down low, if you can. Feet flat, or even sitting on the floor. Bring to mind someone who is hurting right now. Now, in your mind, go and sit down next to them, on the ground, at their level. Don't say anything. No advice, no reasons, no it'll be okay. If words come up, let them pass, the way a car passes outside. Just stay, and keep seeing them. That's the whole of it. The bell holds the time.
Seven days of silence: Job's three friends sit on the ground with him and say nothing, because they saw that his grief was very great. Today's word.
Your line: sit with them. Today, when someone tells you something hard, let one full breath pass before you say anything at all. Sometimes the breath is the answer. Day seven hundred nine.

what a scholar hears: Job 2:11–13: they come 'to mourn with him and to comfort him', and their silence has a stated reason: 'for they saw that his grief was very great.'

710.title: Then the friends talk
710.hook: they explain his suffering as punishment, and God later says they were wrong (Job 4–25; 42:7)
710.howItsDone: Jews and Christians read the speeches of Job's friends in different ways; some readers take them, and God's words in Job 42:7, as a warning against explaining another person's pain.

segments.voice: Yesterday: seven days of silence on the ground. Your line was sit with them. Did you let a full breath pass before you answered someone? Today the silence breaks. Day seven hundred ten.

Job speaks first, and what he says is raw. He curses the day he was born. And that's when his friend Eliphaz can't hold it in any longer. He starts politely, almost shyly: "If we assay to commune with thee, wilt thou be grieved?" In plain words: if we say something, will it upset you? And then he says it anyway. What follows runs on for chapter after chapter, and it begins with a question that sounds like comfort and lands like a verdict.
screen: `JOB CURSES HIS DAY.` → `IF WE SAY SOMETHING, WILL IT HURT?` → `A QUESTION THAT LANDS LIKE A VERDICT.`

segments.voice: First, the friends' theory. Here's Eliphaz's question: "Remember, I pray thee, who ever perished, being innocent? or where were the righteous cut off?" Follow that through. If innocent people don't perish, and Job is perishing, then Job must not be innocent. Bildad and Zophar take their turns, and Eliphaz comes back for more. The details change, but the shape holds: God is just, so suffering points to wrongdoing. Turn back, and things will be restored. Second, Job's answer. He doesn't thank them. "I have heard many such things: miserable comforters are ye all." And at one point he asks for something they've forgotten how to give: "O that ye would altogether hold your peace! and it should be your wisdom." He wants the silence back, the quiet they once kept on the ground beside him. Third, the verdict. At the very end of the book, God turns to Eliphaz and says: "My wrath is kindled against thee, and against thy two friends: for ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath." The careful explainers are told they were wrong. The man who protested, the book says, spoke what is right. Fourth, why the explaining. Some readers notice that the friends' theory protects the friends. If suffering always has a reason, then good behavior is a kind of safety, and what happened to Job can't happen to them. That might be why explanations come so fast, at bedsides and in kitchens. And the book's first chapter and its last both refuse their reason.
screen: `THE THEORY: SUFFERING MEANS SIN.` · `MISERABLE COMFORTERS.` · `GOD SAYS THEY WERE WRONG.` · `AN EXPLANATION CAN PROTECT THE EXPLAINER.` · then, large: `DON'T EXPLAIN IT.`

segments.voice: Sit, and settle. Bring to mind someone whose trouble you know about. A diagnosis, a breakup, a job lost. Now watch your mind. Does it offer an explanation? Well, they did smoke. Well, they never listened. Well, everything happens for a reason. If one comes, notice it, and notice whom it comforts. Then set it down, unspoken, and come back to the person: their face, their day, how heavy it must be. Stay with them instead of the reason. The bell holds the time.
Then the friends talk: Job's friends explain his suffering as punishment, and at the end of the book God says they have not spoken what is right. Today's word.
Your line: don't explain it. Today, when someone shares a trouble, skip the reason and the lesson. Ask one question about how they're doing, or just say that sounds hard. Day seven hundred ten.

711.title: Job argues
711.hook: Job demands a hearing from God, and the book lets him (Job 23)
711.howItsDone: Jews and Christians both keep Job's complaints and Abraham's bargaining in scripture, and some people in both traditions bring honest complaints about what feels unjust into prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday: then the friends talk, and the book's ending says they were wrong. Your line was don't explain it. Did you skip the reason and simply listen? Today Job turns away from his friends and toward God. Day seven hundred eleven.

There's the complaint muttered in the car on the way home, and there's the complaint written up, signed, and filed. One lets off steam. The other asks for an answer, and it names who should give it. Job has had enough of muttering. His friends keep telling him what God must be thinking. So in chapter twenty-three he says it outright: he wants to bring his case to God directly. What he wants is a hearing.
screen: `MUTTERED, OR FILED?` → `DONE TALKING ABOUT GOD.` → `HE WANTS A HEARING.`

segments.voice: First, a case to make. Here's Job: "Oh that I knew where I might find him! that I might come even to his seat! I would order my cause before him, and fill my mouth with arguments." Listen to the words. His cause. His arguments. A seat, like a judge's bench. Job talks like a man with a case, and he wants his day in court. Second, an empty courtroom. The trouble is, he can't find the judge. "Behold, I go forward, but he is not there; and backward, but I cannot perceive him." He looks every way and God is hidden, and Job says so, out loud, in scripture. Third, the book lets him. Job's speeches are long and angry, and some readers find them shocking. The book doesn't soften them to be polite. He said he would fill his mouth with arguments, and the book gives him room to do it, speech after speech, chapter after chapter. The whirlwind will have hard questions for Job, too. But it comes after the speeches, not instead of them, and the speeches stay on the page, in the book that Jews and Christians both read as scripture. Fourth, arguing toward, not away. Notice who Job is talking to. Not about God behind his back, but to God, asking to be heard. Even in the middle of the complaint he says: "But he knoweth the way that I take: when he hath tried me, I shall come forth as gold." Job isn't the only one in the Bible to do this. In Genesis, Abraham bargains with God over the city of Sodom, and asks: "Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right?" Some readers hear in both a kind of faith that argues because it still expects an answer.
screen: `A CASE TO MAKE.` · `HE CAN'T FIND THE JUDGE.` · `THE BOOK LETS IT STAND.` · `ARGUING TOWARD, NOT AWAY.` · then, large: `ARGUE IF YOU MUST.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the jaw unclench. Find one thing in your life that feels unfair. Big or small. Now say it, inwardly, plainly, in a sentence or two. No polishing, no softening, no making it sound nicer than it is. If you pray, you can say it to God, the way Job did. If you don't, say it to the room, or to life itself. Then stop, and sit with it said. Notice what it's like to have it out, instead of held in. The bell holds the time.
Job argues: in chapter twenty-three, Job asks for a hearing before God to lay out his case, and the book lets his complaint stand. Today's word.
Your line: argue if you must. If something is unfair today, say it plainly once, to the one who can actually answer, instead of muttering it to someone who can't. Day seven hundred eleven.

712.title: The whirlwind
712.hook: God answers with stars, sea and wild animals, not with a reason (Job 38–39)
712.howItsDone: Jews and Christians read God's speeches from the whirlwind in Job 38–41 as scripture, and interpret them differently: as rebuke, as comfort, or as a widening of Job's view.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Job argues, and asks for a hearing at God's own seat. Your line was argue if you must. Did you say one unfair thing plainly? Today he gets his hearing, though not the one he asked for. Day seven hundred twelve.

What would you say if you finally got the meeting? Job has had chapter after chapter to prepare. He has his case. He has his arguments. He has signed his name to it, so to speak, and waited. And then, after all the talking, the voice he's been asking for arrives, and not quietly. "Then the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind." Job has a question. What comes back from the storm is a long list of questions of its own.
screen: `JOB HAS HIS CASE READY.` → `THE VOICE ARRIVES.` → `OUT OF THE WHIRLWIND.`

segments.voice: First, questions for questions. The very first thing God asks: "Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth? declare, if thou hast understanding." Not an accusation of sin. A question about scale. Second, stars and sea. The questions keep coming, and they're beautiful. When the earth's cornerstone was laid, "When the morning stars sang together, and all the sons of God shouted for joy?" Who shut in the sea, and told it: "Hitherto shalt thou come, but no further: and here shall thy proud waves be stayed"? Can you bind the Pleiades, or loosen the bands of Orion? Third, animals nobody tamed. Then the speech turns to creatures. The wild donkey who laughs at the noise of the city. The wild ox who won't be harnessed. The ostrich. The war horse: "hast thou clothed his neck with thunder?" The hawk: "Doth the hawk fly by thy wisdom, and stretch her wings toward the south?" A whole world going about its business with no human in charge of it. Fourth, no reason, and still an answer. What's missing is the reason. God never mentions the scene in heaven from chapter one. Job is never told why. And yet Job's reply, near the end, is this: "I have heard of thee by the hearing of the ear: but now mine eye seeth thee." Readers have heard the whirlwind in different ways. Some hear a rebuke, putting Job in his place. Some hear comfort, that the world is held by someone bigger than the question. Some hear an invitation out of the ash heap and into a much wider world. The book doesn't settle it. It answers the argument by showing Job the world.
screen: `QUESTIONS FOR QUESTIONS.` · `STARS SING, THE SEA STOPS.` · `ANIMALS NOBODY TAMED.` · `NO REASON, AND STILL AN ANSWER.` · then, large: `WHERE WERE YOU.`

segments.voice: Find something wild to look at. Through a window, if you can: a tree, a bird, the sky, weather. If not, a houseplant, or the grain in a wooden table, or your own breath, which goes on without your permission. Look at it the whole time. Let it be bigger than your questions, just for now. Notice that it doesn't need you to run it. If a question about your own life comes up, let it sit alongside the wild thing, not on top of it. The bell holds the time.
The whirlwind: out of the storm God answers Job with stars, sea and wild animals, a long run of questions, and not with a reason. Today's word.
Your line: where were you. Step outside once today, find one wild thing, a bird, a weed in a crack, the wind, and let it go on without you for a full minute. Day seven hundred twelve.

713.title: How long?
713.hook: the Psalms let the faithful complain: how long, O Lord? (Psalm 13)
713.howItsDone: Jews and Christians pray the Psalms, alone and together; psalms of complaint like Psalm 13 are part of that prayer, and some people pray them in times of illness, grief or long waiting.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the whirlwind, stars and sea and the hawk heading south. Your line was where were you. Did one wild thing go on without you for a minute? Today we leave Job for the Psalms. Day seven hundred thirteen.

"Are we there yet?" From the back seat, the first time, it's almost cute. By the fourth time, it's a different question. It isn't really asking about the map anymore. It's saying: this is too long, I'm tired, and I don't know if it ends. Grown-ups ask it too, in hospital corridors, in long months out of work, at three in the morning. And the book of Psalms, a book of prayers, keeps that question right inside it.
screen: `ARE WE THERE YET?` → `BY THE FOURTH TIME, A DIFFERENT QUESTION.` → `THE PSALMS KEEP IT.`

segments.voice: First, four times. Psalm thirteen opens: "How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD? for ever? how long wilt thou hide thy face from me?" And the next verse keeps going: "How long shall I take counsel in my soul, having sorrow in my heart daily? how long shall mine enemy be exalted over me?" Count them. How long, four times, in two verses. It's the back seat, at the fourth asking. Second, for ever? Tucked into the first line is the fear underneath the question. Not just how long, but: is this forever? Has God forgotten me for good? The psalm says that out loud, to God, in a prayer. Third, a complaint in the prayer book. This isn't a private diary that slipped in by mistake. The psalm sits in the book of prayers that Jews and Christians both pray. Its heading gives it to the chief musician, as a psalm of David. Complaint, here, is part of worship. In this prayer a faithful voice says to God: are you hiding, and how long? Fourth, the turn. Then, near the end, the psalm turns: "But I have trusted in thy mercy; my heart shall rejoice in thy salvation." And the last line: "I will sing unto the LORD, because he hath dealt bountifully with me." Now look closely. The psalm never says the trouble ended. The enemy isn't said to have left. The sorrow isn't said to be gone. The turn to trust comes inside the waiting, not after it. Some readers hear that as the heart of the psalm: the how long and the but I have trusted, side by side, in one short prayer.
screen: `HOW LONG, FOUR TIMES.` · `FOR EVER?` · `A COMPLAINT IN THE PRAYER BOOK.` · `THE TURN COMES INSIDE THE WAITING.` · then, large: `HOW LONG.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath be slow. Find one thing in your life that's taking too long. A healing, an answer, a change, a person coming round. Now form your own how long, one honest sentence, starting with those two words. If there's paper nearby, write it down; if not, write it in your head, word by word. Read it back once. Then leave it on the page, unanswered. No need to add a happy ending. The bell holds the time.
How long?: the question Psalm thirteen asks four times, a faithful person's complaint kept right inside the book of prayers. Today's word.
Your line: how long. Today, when some waiting wears on you, say how long once, honestly, under your breath, and notice what exactly you're waiting for. Day seven hundred thirteen.

714.title: Out of the depths
714.hook: a psalm that starts at the bottom and waits for morning (Psalm 130)
714.carry: more than watchmen for the morning
714.howItsDone: Jews and Christians pray Psalm 130, alone and in worship, and some people in both traditions turn to it in times of distress or grief.

segments.voice: Yesterday: how long?, asked four times in a short psalm. Your line was how long. Did you say it once, honestly, about some waiting? Today, the end of the week, and a psalm that begins at the very bottom. Day seven hundred fourteen.

Four in the morning at a shut-up warehouse. The night guard walks the loading dock and looks east, over the rooftops. Still black. He finishes his round, pours coffee from a flask, looks east again. Still black. Somewhere a dog barks. Nobody on that shift can make the sun come up any faster. All anyone can do is keep watch, and look east, and wait. There's a psalm built exactly like that night.
screen: `FOUR IN THE MORNING ON THE NIGHT SHIFT.` → `THE EAST IS STILL BLACK.` → `A PSALM BUILT LIKE THAT NIGHT.`

segments.voice: First, from the bottom. Psalm one hundred thirty opens: "Out of the depths have I cried unto thee, O LORD." No warm-up, no praise first. The singer is already down there, calling up. Second, no scorecard. Then a surprise: "If thou, LORD, shouldest mark iniquities, O Lord, who shall stand? But there is forgiveness with thee, that thou mayest be feared." If God kept a strict ledger, nobody would be left standing. And the psalm answers its own question: there is forgiveness. It's a different picture from the one Job's friends drew, where every suffering had a line in the ledger. Third, waiting for morning. "I wait for the LORD, my soul doth wait, and in his word do I hope. My soul waiteth for the Lord more than they that watch for the morning: I say, more than they that watch for the morning." The psalm says it twice, like someone looking east a second time. Another old translation puts it: more than watchmen for the morning. The watchmen can't hurry the dawn. They can only keep watch, sure it's coming. Fourth, the week. Look at what this week held. Job lost everything, and the reader knew it wasn't deserved. His friends sat seven days in silence, and then they talked, and were wrong. Job argued, and asked for a hearing. The whirlwind answered with stars and hawks. Psalm thirteen asked how long. And now this: a cry from the depths, and a long wait for the light. Not one of them explains suffering away. Each one finds a way to speak from inside it.

segments.voice: Sit, and let your weight sink down. Find the lowest place in you right now. It may be deep, or just a little low. Don't climb out of it yet. Instead, keep watch from there, the way the guard keeps watch. On each in-breath, look east, in your mind, toward where the light will come. On each out-breath, let the dark be dark a little longer. No forcing the dawn. If your attention wanders, come back and look east again, the way the psalm says its line a second time. The bell holds the time.
